TRACE for Everyone

A Simple Guide to Better Decisions

TRACE is a practical tool that helps you think through big decisions by looking at how they affect different areas of your life over time. Think of it like a GPS for life choices—it shows you where different paths lead before you commit to them.

The name TRACE stands for five questions you ask about any major decision: Time (how will this play out over time?), Resources (what am I really trading here?), Affected (who and what else does this impact?), Capacity (does this make me stronger or weaker?), and Exit (can I change course if needed?).

We all face tough choices—job offers, relationship decisions, where to live, how to spend our time. Usually we go with our gut or make a quick pros/cons list. But life is more complex than that. TRACE helps you see the full picture, including things you might miss. It's especially useful when you're considering something that looks great short-term but might have hidden long-term costs, or when you need to do something intense for a while but want to make sure you don't get stuck.

Before You Start: Know Your Destination

Before analyzing options, get clear on your bigger goals. Not just "make more money" but what you want your life to look like in 5-10 years. Maybe it's being healthy and energetic enough to play with your kids, having the skills to start your own business, building relationships that support you through tough times, or contributing to causes you care about.

List out your choices, but think beyond just "Option A or B." Consider whether you can do something intense for a short time then switch, whether you can combine different approaches, or what a middle ground might look like.

Time: How Will This Play Out?

Play the movie forward. If you choose this path, what does your life look like in 6 months? 2 years? 5 years? Red flags to watch for include thinking "I'll do this crazy schedule just for a year" but having no clear exit plan, believing "things will get easier once I..." but that milestone keeps moving, or assuming "I can always change later" but each month makes it harder to leave.

Green flags include having clear phases with an intense period leading to a specific goal followed by a transition plan, situations that get easier over time rather than harder, and choices that build options rather than closing them.

Resources: What Am I Really Trading?

Money is just one resource. Also consider time (once spent, you can't get it back), health (stress and exhaustion compound over time), relationships (they need regular investment or they fade), skills (they grow with use or shrink with neglect), and reputation (built slowly, lost quickly).

The key question is whether you're trading renewable resources for permanent gains, or burning permanent resources for temporary rewards.

Affected: Who Else Is in the Boat?

Your decisions create ripples. Your family adapts to your schedule, with your spouse adjusting their life and kids experiencing your availability or absence. Friends need relationship maintenance or connections drift apart. Colleagues feel the effects of your choices through team dynamics. Your community notices your participation or absence in various ways.

Ask yourself who has to adjust their life to make your choice work, which relationships can handle temporary strain, and what support systems you're depending on.

Capacity: Am I Building or Burning?

Some choices make you stronger over time, others wear you down. Building patterns include learning new skills that open doors, saving money that creates options, developing relationships that provide support, and maintaining health that sustains everything else.

Burning patterns include using up savings with no replacement plan, exhausting yourself with no recovery time, isolating from support networks, and developing habits that limit future choices.

Exit: Can I Change Course?

The "golden handcuffs" test asks whether you're maintaining freedom to pivot or getting locked in. Warning signs of getting trapped include lifestyle inflation that requires high income, skills getting outdated while you're too busy to learn, your network shrinking to only your current environment, health declining so other options seem impossible, and your identity becoming tied to your current situation.

Maintaining options means living below your means even when earning more, keeping skills sharp and learning new ones, maintaining diverse friendships and connections, protecting your health as non-negotiable, and remembering you're more than your job or role.

Putting It All Together

Let's see TRACE in action with two job offers. Job A is a startup offering big money but expecting 70-hour weeks. Job B is an established company with lower pay but work-life balance.

Looking at time, Job A might fund your goals faster, but can you sustain the pace? Job B builds steadily. For resources, Job A trades health and relationships for money while Job B trades some income for everything else. Regarding affected systems, Job A means your partner handles all home duties while Job B allows shared responsibilities. For capacity, Job A might burn you out while Job B lets you learn, exercise, and maintain relationships. Considering exit options, Job A's high pay might trap you in expensive habits while Job B keeps options open.

The insight might be to take Job A for exactly 18 months to hit a specific financial goal, then transition to something sustainable. Or recognize that Job B better serves your long-term vision despite lower immediate rewards.

Smart Patterns to Consider

The Sprint and Recover pattern involves working intensely toward a specific goal, then shifting to recovery mode, like athletes who train hard then rest. The key is defining the finish line before you start.

The Portfolio Approach balances different activities—some for money, some for growth, some for relationships. No single choice has to be perfect when you're building a diversified life portfolio.

The Step-by-Step pattern builds toward your ideal gradually, with each phase creating the foundation for the next.

Quick Decision Check

For any big choice, ask whether this decision has a clear timeframe or is indefinite. Consider whether you're building something lasting or just consuming resources. Think about whether the people you care about can handle the impact. Evaluate whether you'll be stronger or weaker in five years. Check whether you can change direction if this doesn't work out.

TRACE isn't about finding perfect answers—life's too complex for that. It's about seeing the full picture before you choose. Sometimes you need to do something difficult short-term to set up long-term success. Sometimes the "lesser" option is actually better for the life you want to build.

The goal is making choices with eyes wide open, understanding the real trade-offs, and designing strategies that help you thrive over time rather than just survive the moment.

Start Small

Try TRACE on a medium-size decision first. Should you take that evening class? Join that committee? Start that side project? Practice seeing how choices ripple through time and systems. Soon it becomes natural to think this way about bigger decisions.

Your future self will thank you for thinking beyond tomorrow.
